I have been farming this 5-mu plot in Quzhou for 25 years, and I know every corner of it. My family has four mouths to feed, and with some of us working off-farm, I cannot afford to waste labor on unnecessary work. At 42, I have learned that this North China Plain soil rewards steady, practical management—not fancy experiments.

This autumn, I will plant winter wheat on all 5 mu because the wheat-maize rotation is what this land and climate demand. I will buy improved wheat seed from the county supply shop; I do not trust saved seed anymore because the yield drops after a few generations. For fertilizer, I will spread compound fertilizer as a base dose and then top-dress with urea at green-up and jointing—about 16 kg of nitrogen per mu in total, plus 7 kg phosphorus and 5 kg potassium. My well gives reliable water, but electricity costs money, so I will irrigate three times: at planting if the soil is dry, at jointing in spring, and once more at grain filling. I will do rotary tillage before wheat planting to bury the maize stubble and level the field.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I need to get the summer maize in quickly before the season slips away. I will plant hybrid maize seed—hybrids pay for themselves every time. I will apply about 15 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu, and because some family members are busy with off-farm jobs, I will use no-tillage planting right behind the combine to save time and keep soil moisture. I will irrigate twice if the summer rains are normal: at the big trumpet stage and at filling. For both crops, I will spray herbicide once and watch for insects, giving wheat two pesticide applications and maize two as well.

I expect about 500 kg of wheat per mu and around 550 kg of maize per mu in a normal year. These numbers have been consistent for me when I do not cut corners on the basics.
